content: In recent years, there has been an increase in the number of women participating in the workforce. Some of these women may become pregnant while employed and later give birth. Many of them may choose to return to work relatively soon after giving birth for a variety of reasons. However, without adequate support from their employers and colleagues, these mothers may discontinue breastfeeding upon their return to work. This lack of support can negatively impact both the duration and exclusivity of breastfeeding, which is recommended for the optimal health of the baby. The workplace environment has the potential to play a significant role in encouraging and facilitating breastfeeding. For women who return to work after childbirth, there are various types of workplace interventions available that can support breastfeeding. Employers should not overlook the importance of implementing such measures. Promoting breastfeeding in the workplace can yield benefits not only for the mother and her child but also for the employer, such as improved employee satisfaction and potentially reduced absenteeism. The objective of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness of workplace interventions designed to support and promote breastfeeding among women returning to paid employment after childbirth. Additionally, the study aimed to assess the impact of these interventions on outcomes relevant to both employees and employers. To conduct this evaluation, a search was performed in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register on August 2, 2012. The selection criteria included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared workplace interventions with either no intervention or with other workplace interventions. Two authors independently reviewed all identified studies to determine their eligibility. The authors planned to assess the methodological quality of the eligible trials and extract relevant data. However, no randomized controlled trials or quasi-randomized controlled trials were identified during the search. As a result, the authors concluded that there is currently no evidence from trials to evaluate the effectiveness of workplace interventions in promoting breastfeeding among women returning to paid work after childbirth. Furthermore, the impact of such interventions on process outcomes remains unknown. To address this gap, randomized controlled trials are necessary to determine the benefits of various workplace interventions aimed at supporting, encouraging, and promoting breastfeeding among working mothers.
